one_line: Local-model buying guide by GPU tier: context budget (KV cache) and read speed matter more than which model you pick. Covers quantization pitfalls, two free speed settings, and when renting beats owning.
summary: The host argues that local model tier lists ignore the KV cache, the per-token memory that grows with context and competes with the weights for VRAM. From 12 to 48 GB he says the same 27B-class model applies throughout, and what changes is how much context fits and how fast the card can re-read it. He walks through hardware tiers from 4 GB up to 128 GB and beyond, flagging quantization traps such as 4-bit builds not fitting 16 GB, and 2-bit uploads from different compressors differing sharply in bug-fixing results. He recommends two free settings, multi-token prediction and a medium rather than maximum reasoning level, which he reports as large speedups with little quality loss. Above 128 GB he says prompt reading speed becomes the bottleneck, and at that scale renting is cheaper than owning. His evidence is mostly forum posts, Reddit threads and single-person runs rather than controlled benchmarks, so the numbers are indicative only.

key_ideas.idea: The same model applies from 12 GB to 48 GB; what changes is how much code fits in context and how fast it is read. Model choice is largely settled, so context capacity is the real currency.
key_ideas.detail: Tier lists match model size to VRAM and skip the KV cache. The host reframes the question as how much context you can afford.

key_ideas.idea: The KV cache is ongoing rent, not a one-time deposit. Every file, error log and test output the agent reads adds to memory that keeps growing.
key_ideas.detail: Loading the weights is a one-time cost, but the cache sits in the same VRAM and expands with every token of context.

key_ideas.idea: Architecture decides KV cost at equal parameter count. A 27B model where only 16 of 64 layers grow with context fits 128k context in under 9 GB, while a similar 24B Mistral model with all layers growing needs over 21 GB.
key_ideas.detail: Check the layer mix before assuming two same-size models cost the same to run at long context.

key_ideas.idea: Harness overhead spends the context window before the user types anything. Instructions and tool definitions load first, and a lean harness matters on small cards.
key_ideas.detail: The host cites a Reddit report of three MCP connections costing 3-5k tokens up front, and default setups giving only about 4k context on smaller cards.

key_ideas.idea: On 8 GB, a dense 27B model spilling into system RAM runs at about 4-5 tokens/s, which is unusable for agents. A mixture-of-experts model with most weights in RAM reached about 26 tokens/s on an older 8 GB card with 32 GB RAM, but tool-calling failure rates were worse.
key_ideas.detail: The trade-off is speed for reliability. The host calls the MoE choice the tool that fits, not the sharpest one.

key_ideas.idea: At 16 GB, a 3-bit 27B build (about 13 GB) fits where the standard 4-bit build (about 17.4 GB) does not. An independent benchmark found the 3-bit build scoring nearly the same as full size on real coding tasks.
key_ideas.detail: The 16 GB advice is to use an aggressive quant rather than the generic 4-bit recommendation.

key_ideas.idea: Quantized builds of the same model differ a lot by who compressed them. Two 2-bit uploads on the same bug-fixing tasks differed by more than 2x in bugs solved.
key_ideas.detail: Pick quant uploads by testing them on your own tasks, not by name or bit width alone.

key_ideas.idea: Two free settings beat many hardware upgrades. Multi-token prediction, toggled by one flag, raised one benchmark from 48 to 76 tokens/s on a high-end card and from 74 to 180 on the newest desktop card. Dropping reasoning from max to medium gave similar scores in community tests.
key_ideas.detail: The host says Apple Silicon gets no multi-token benefit because some conversion tools strip the feature. Max reasoning took 21 minutes on one drawing prompt versus about 2 minutes with reasoning off.

key_ideas.idea: Above 128 GB, the bottleneck is reading speed, not memory size. A mini PC got about 50 tokens/s generation, but a full prompt reload took over a minute. Four modded GPUs cut that reload to seconds.
key_ideas.detail: Agents re-read files and error output constantly, so prefill speed can dominate wall-clock time more than generation speed.

key_ideas.idea: Owning hardware only pays off for one buyer: someone who would otherwise rent a 27B model constantly. A 24-32 GB card pays back in about a year of daily use. Renting beats owning at larger scales, and NDA-bound work stays local.
key_ideas.detail: Large-model hosting costs pennies per million output tokens, about 10x cheaper than renting the 27B model. Two workstation boxes were estimated at roughly six years to break even. The host recommends a frontier model for planning and a local model for well-defined tasks.

techniques.name: Budget the KV cache per context length, not just model size
techniques.how: Look up how many layers keep per-token state. Estimate KV GB at your target context (the host uses 64k and 128k) and subtract it from VRAM left after the weights. Compare models of the same parameter count on this number.
techniques.when: Choosing a model or quantization for a given card, especially for agent workloads with large context.

techniques.name: Set the context window explicitly
techniques.how: Override the default context size in your local server instead of accepting the harness default, and size it to what the card can hold alongside the weights.
techniques.when: Any local agent run. The host says defaults can be as low as about 4k on smaller cards.

techniques.name: Cut harness overhead before the first prompt
techniques.how: Measure tokens used by system instructions and tool definitions before any user input. Remove unused MCP connections (the host cites 3-5k tokens for three). Keep instruction files short.
techniques.when: Local models with limited context windows, where fixed overhead eats a large share of the budget.

techniques.name: Enable multi-token prediction
techniques.how: Turn on the model's multi-token prediction feature with a single flag. The video does not name the flag, so check the inference server's docs for the exact option.
techniques.when: NVIDIA-class GPUs. The host reports no benefit on Apple Silicon, where some conversion tools remove the feature.

techniques.name: Use medium reasoning effort instead of the max default
techniques.how: Set the model's reasoning level to medium rather than the shipped maximum. The host reports near-identical scores on community tests at a fraction of the thinking time.
techniques.when: Interactive coding agents where latency matters and the tasks are well-scoped.

techniques.name: Vet quantized builds on your own tasks
techniques.how: Run the same bug-fixing or coding task set against each candidate community quant, then compare the results with the hosted API score for the same model before choosing one.
techniques.when: Choosing 2-bit or 3-bit builds, where the same model and bit width can perform very differently between uploaders.

techniques.name: Run a mixture-of-experts model with experts offloaded to RAM on 8 GB cards
techniques.how: Use a MoE model where only a small set of experts is active per token. Keep the bulk of weights in system RAM and the active parts on GPU. Accept weaker long tool-calling reliability.
techniques.when: An 8 GB card with about 32 GB of system RAM, where a dense model would spill and run at a few tokens/s.

techniques.name: Split planning from execution across frontier and local models
techniques.how: Use a frontier model for planning and architecture, and hand well-defined, mechanical sub-tasks to a local model.
techniques.when: Code that cannot leave the building under NDA or compliance rules, or cost-sensitive workloads that still need strong planning.

techniques.name: Track prefill (read) speed separately from generation speed
techniques.how: Measure time to process a full prompt reload alongside tokens/s for generation. For agent loops that re-read files and logs, prefill often dominates wall-clock time.
techniques.when: Sizing hardware above about 128 GB or comparing a mini PC against a multi-GPU rig.

numbers.claim: Rule of thumb: a compressed model needs about 0.5 GB of memory per billion parameters (27B is about 24 GB).
27B model with 16 of 64 layers growing: 128k context costs under 9 GB. Similar 24B Mistral with all layers growing: over 21 GB for the same context.
Three MCP tool connections cost 3-5k tokens before any work starts (anecdote from a Reddit thread). Default setups on smaller cards give about 4k context.
27B model spilled into system RAM on an 8 GB card runs at about 4-5 tokens/s.
MoE model with experts in RAM on a 2016-era 8 GB card with 32 GB RAM: about 26 tokens/s, about 5x the spill setup.
27B 4-bit build is about 17.4 GB and does not fit 16 GB. The 3-bit build is about 13 GB.
On 12 GB, 2-bit builds are needed. Two 2-bit uploads on the same bug-fix tasks: one matched the hosted API score, the other solved less than half as many bugs.
On 24 GB, the 4-bit build needs about 22 GB at 64k context. At 32 GB, full context fits. At 48 GB, 8-bit is possible.
Desktop high-end card launched under $2,000 and is selling for over $6,000. A laptop variant has 24 GB vs 32 GB on the desktop and runs at roughly half the benchmark speed.
Multi-token prediction: 48 to 76 tokens/s on a high-end card; 74 to 180 tokens/s on the newest desktop card.
Max reasoning: 21 minutes on one drawing prompt vs about 2 minutes with reasoning off (9x). Medium reasoning scores almost identically to max in a week of community testing.
Larger MoE model at 4-bit needs about 111 GB. A mini PC gets about 50 tokens/s generation, but a full prompt reload can take over a minute.
Hosting the much larger model costs pennies per million output tokens, about 10x cheaper than renting the 27B model. Two workstation boxes estimated at about six years to break even vs renting.
A 24-32 GB card pays for itself in about a year of regular daily use versus renting the 27B model, before electricity.

hot_takes: Per-card model tier lists ignore the KV cache, so the 'same model from 12 to 48 GB' framing matters more than any single benchmark. Most of the evidence is forum posts and single-person runs, not controlled tests.
Running a 27B model on 8 GB at 4-5 tokens/s is dismissed as 'watching paint dry', even though the video that showed it got about half a million views.
Multi-token prediction gives no benefit on Apple Silicon, according to the host, because some conversion tools strip the feature.
Owning a GPU only pays off for a heavy daily user of a 24-32 GB model. For most people, renting is the better economics, and NDA-bound code should stay local.
Free hosted endpoints rarely stay private, so don't send NDA material to them.

relevance.why: InferCraft is vLLM on one RTX 5090 (32 GB) with pluggable KV-cache strategies and speculative decoding. The video's central point is that KV-cache growth, per-layer cache design and quant quality decide what fits, and it names multi-token prediction as a near-free speedup. It is not a benchmark for AgentOS itself.
relevance.action: Measure KV bytes per 128k context for the served 27B-class model on the 5090, comparing its layer mix against the claim that only a fraction of layers grow. Use the result to choose between quant and KV strategies in InferCraft before picking a config.

relevance.why: The harness overhead point (instructions and tool definitions consume context before work starts) matters for a Claude Code wrapper. The video's advice is generic and doesn't address Claude Code specifically.
relevance.action: Log how many tokens ProsHarness's system prompt, CLAUDE.md and enabled MCP tools consume before the first user turn, and trim anything unused.
